terms.definition: A number a + bi with real part a and imaginary part b, where i² = −1. Quantum amplitudes are complex numbers.
The modulus of a complex number z = a + bi is |z| = √(a² + b²), its distance from the origin in the complex plane. The squared modulus of an amplitude gives a probability.
Writing a complex number as r·e^{iφ}, with modulus r and angle φ. It makes the phase of an amplitude explicit.
A factor e^{iγ} multiplying a whole state vector. It changes no measurement probability, so states that differ only by a global phase are physically identical.
The phase difference between the amplitudes of two basis states in a superposition, as in (|0⟩ + e^{iφ}|1⟩)/√2. It is not observable directly but decides the outcome of interference.
For column vectors, ⟨u|v⟩ is the sum of the conjugated entries of u times the entries of v. Its squared modulus gives the probability of finding |v⟩ in the state |u⟩.
The requirement that the squared moduli of a state's amplitudes add up to 1, so that the measurement probabilities sum to 1.
A matrix U with U†U = I. Unitaries preserve the norm of a state and describe every reversible quantum operation.
The matrix A† obtained by transposing A and conjugating every entry. Also called the Hermitian adjoint.
A matrix equal to its own conjugate transpose, A = A†. Its eigenvalues are real, so it represents an observable.
The matrices X, Y and Z, which with the identity I form a basis for all 2×2 matrices. They are Hermitian and unitary and square to I.
For a matrix A, a number λ with A|v⟩ = λ|v⟩ for some nonzero vector |v⟩, called an eigenvector. Eigenvalues of a unitary are phases e^{iφ}.
The operation ⊗ that combines the state spaces of two systems. The state of n qubits lives in the n-fold tensor product of C².
A multi-qubit state that can be written as a tensor product of single-qubit states. Any state that cannot be written this way is entangled.
The basic unit of quantum information: a two-level system whose state is a unit vector α|0⟩ + β|1⟩ in C².
The orthonormal basis {|0⟩, |1⟩} of one qubit, or the 2ⁿ bit-string states |x⟩ of n qubits. Measurement in this basis returns a bit string.
The column vector of complex amplitudes that describes the pure state of a quantum system.
A complex coefficient of a basis state in a state vector. The probability of an outcome is the squared modulus of its amplitude (Born rule).
A state described by a single state vector |ψ⟩, or equivalently a density operator with purity Tr(ρ²) = 1.
The unit sphere whose points represent the pure states of one qubit up to global phase. |0⟩ and |1⟩ sit at the poles and single-qubit gates act as rotations.
The Pauli X gate swaps |0⟩ and |1⟩. It is the quantum NOT and a rotation by π about the x-axis of the Bloch sphere.
A state that is a linear combination of basis states with more than one nonzero amplitude, such as (|0⟩ + |1⟩)/√2.
The single-qubit gate H that maps |0⟩ to |+⟩ and |1⟩ to |−⟩. It converts between the computational basis and the ± basis.
An operation that extracts a classical outcome from a quantum state with probabilities given by the Born rule and leaves the state collapsed to the outcome.
The gate S = diag(1, i), a quarter turn about the z-axis. It adds a relative phase of π/2 to |1⟩.
The gates R_x(θ), R_y(θ) and R_z(θ), which rotate the Bloch vector by the angle θ about the x, y or z axis.
The effect by which amplitudes of different computational paths add or cancel, depending on their relative phase. Quantum algorithms arrange for wrong answers to cancel.
A property of multi-qubit states that cannot be written as a product of single-qubit states. Measurement outcomes of the parts are correlated beyond classical means.
The four maximally entangled two-qubit states |Φ⁺⟩, |Φ⁻⟩, |Ψ⁺⟩ and |Ψ⁻⟩, which form an orthonormal basis of two qubits.
The two-qubit gate that flips the target qubit when the control qubit is |1⟩. With H, it creates Bell states from basis states.
The qubit whose value decides whether a controlled operation acts on the target qubit.
A gate that applies a unitary U to a target qubit only when a control qubit is |1⟩, acting as a coherent if-statement on basis states.
A protocol that transfers an unknown qubit state using a shared Bell pair and two classical bits, without moving the physical qubit.
The theorem that no quantum operation can copy an arbitrary unknown state: there is no unitary with U|ψ⟩|0⟩ = |ψ⟩|ψ⟩ for all |ψ⟩.
A protocol in which one qubit of a shared Bell pair carries two classical bits from a sender to a receiver.
A two-player cooperative game in which classical strategies win at most 75% of the time, while players sharing an entangled pair can win about 85.4%.
A black-box unitary U_f that computes a function f, mapping |x⟩|y⟩ to |x⟩|y ⊕ f(x)⟩. Algorithms are judged by how many times they query it.
One use of an oracle. Query complexity counts how many such uses an algorithm needs.
The effect that a controlled-U acting on an eigenstate of U leaves that eigenstate unchanged and writes its eigenvalue as a phase onto the control qubit.
A Boolean function f whose output is the same for every input. In the Deutsch–Jozsa problem the other allowed case is a balanced function.
A Boolean function that outputs 0 for exactly half of its inputs and 1 for the other half.
A one-query algorithm that decides whether a one-bit function is constant or balanced, where a classical algorithm needs two queries.
An algorithm that decides with one query whether an n-bit function is constant or balanced, where a deterministic classical algorithm needs 2ⁿ⁻¹ + 1 queries.
An algorithm that finds a hidden bit string s of the function f(x) = s·x mod 2 with a single query.
Given a function with f(x) = f(x ⊕ s) for a hidden string s, find s. Simon's algorithm needs O(n) queries, while classical algorithms need exponentially many.
One round of Grover's algorithm: an oracle that flips the phase of the marked states followed by the diffusion operator.
A search algorithm that finds a marked item among N using about (π/4)√N oracle queries, a quadratic speedup over classical search.
The operator 2|s⟩⟨s| − I, where |s⟩ is the uniform superposition. It reflects every amplitude about the mean amplitude.
The unitary that maps a basis state |x⟩ to a superposition of all basis states with phases e^{2πixy/N}. It is the quantum analogue of the discrete Fourier transform.
An algorithm that estimates the phase φ in an eigenvalue e^{2πiφ} of a unitary U, given an eigenstate, using controlled powers of U and an inverse QFT.
The problem of finding the smallest r > 0 with aʳ ≡ 1 (mod N). It is solved by phase estimation and is the quantum core of Shor's algorithm.
The smallest r > 0 such that f(x + r) = f(x) for all x. Order finding in Shor's algorithm is period finding; Simon's problem uses a period under bitwise XOR, f(x ⊕ s) = f(x).
A quantum algorithm that factors integers in polynomial time by reducing factoring to order finding.
A Hermitian operator H that represents the energy of a system and generates its time evolution e^{−iHt}.
A method that approximates e^{−i(A+B)t} by alternating short evolutions under A and B. The error shrinks as the number of steps grows.
The average result ⟨ψ|O|ψ⟩ of measuring an observable O on the state |ψ⟩, estimated by repeated measurement.
A parameterized circuit family whose parameters are tuned by a classical optimizer in a variational algorithm.
A rule that gives the exact gradient of an expectation value with respect to a rotation angle from two shifted evaluations: [f(θ + π/2) − f(θ − π/2)]/2.
The eigenstate of a Hamiltonian with the lowest energy eigenvalue.
A variational algorithm that estimates the ground-state energy of a Hamiltonian by minimizing the expectation value ⟨ψ(θ)|H|ψ(θ)⟩ over an ansatz.
The fact that the expectation value of H in any state is at least the ground-state energy, so minimizing it gives an upper bound.
A variational algorithm that alternates a cost Hamiltonian evolution and a mixer Hamiltonian evolution to find good solutions of combinatorial problems.
The problem of splitting the vertices of a graph into two sets to maximize the number of edges between them.
A Hamiltonian whose ground state encodes the optimal solution of a problem, such as the Max-Cut cost operator.
The Hamiltonian, usually a sum of X terms, whose evolution moves amplitude between bit strings in QAOA.
A model design in which the input data is encoded repeatedly between trainable layers, increasing the expressive power of a small circuit.
A parameterized circuit trained to assign class labels to data encoded in qubits, with the label read from a measurement.
The operator ρ that describes a quantum state, pure or mixed, with ρ ≥ 0 and Tr(ρ) = 1. Probabilities follow from Tr(ρP) for a projector P.
A statistical mixture of pure states, with a density operator ρ = Σ pᵢ|ψᵢ⟩⟨ψᵢ|. It arises from classical ignorance or from entanglement with an unobserved system.
The quantity Tr(ρ²). It equals 1 for a pure state and is smaller for a mixed state, down to 1/d for the maximally mixed state of dimension d.
A completely positive, trace-preserving map ρ → E(ρ) that describes the evolution of an open quantum system, including noise.
Operators Kₖ with Σ Kₖ†Kₖ = I that define a channel by E(ρ) = Σ KₖρKₖ†.
A channel that applies X with probability p and does nothing otherwise.
A channel that applies Z with probability p and does nothing otherwise. It destroys superpositions without changing populations.
A channel that replaces the state with the maximally mixed state with probability p, equivalent to applying X, Y or Z at random.
A channel that models energy loss, sending |1⟩ to |0⟩ with probability γ. It is the standard model of T1 relaxation.
Loss of phase coherence between |0⟩ and |1⟩ without energy loss. It is the standard model of T2 decay.
The relaxation time of a qubit: the characteristic time for an excited |1⟩ to decay to |0⟩.
The dephasing time of a qubit: the characteristic time over which superpositions lose their phase coherence. It satisfies T2 ≤ 2·T1.
The use of redundancy across several physical qubits to detect and undo errors without measuring the encoded information.
A code that encodes a|0⟩ + b|1⟩ as a|000⟩ + b|111⟩ and corrects any single bit flip by majority vote.
The outcome of parity checks that reveal which error occurred without revealing the encoded state.
A qubit encoded in the joint state of several physical qubits, protected by an error-correcting code.
The Hadamard-conjugated version of the bit-flip code, encoding in |+++⟩ and |−−−⟩ to correct a single phase flip.
The nine-qubit code that concatenates the phase-flip and bit-flip codes and corrects an arbitrary single-qubit error.
A Pauli operator S with S|ψ⟩ = |ψ⟩. A stabilizer code is defined as the joint +1 eigenspace of a set of commuting stabilizers.
The minimum number of physical qubits on which a logical operator acts nontrivially. A code of distance d corrects up to ⌊(d−1)/2⌋ errors.
A topological stabilizer code on a lattice with periodic boundaries, whose stabilizers are local star and plaquette operators.
The result that if the physical error rate per operation is below a threshold, arbitrarily long computations can be made reliable with polynomial overhead.
Designing circuits so that a single fault cannot spread into an uncorrectable error in the encoded data.
The process of rewriting a circuit into the native gates and connectivity of a specific device, while optimizing it.
The graph of which pairs of physical qubits can interact directly with a two-qubit gate on a device.
The gate set a device implements directly. All other gates are decomposed into it during transpilation.
A two-qubit gate that exchanges the states of two qubits. Transpilers insert SWAPs to connect qubits that are not adjacent.
The Qiskit interfaces Sampler, which returns measurement samples, and Estimator, which returns expectation values of observables.
The number of times a circuit is run and measured to collect outcome statistics.
A Hermitian operator whose eigenvalues are the possible measurement results and whose expectation value predicts their average.
The probability that a measurement reports the wrong bit. It is one of the main sources of error on current devices.
The average infidelity of a gate on hardware, typically much larger for two-qubit gates than for single-qubit gates.
Techniques that reduce the bias of noisy expectation values without a quantum code, using extra circuit runs (for example gate folding) and classical post-processing.
A mitigation method that runs a circuit at several amplified noise levels and extrapolates the expectation value to zero noise.
A description of the errors of a device as a set of channels attached to gates and measurements, used in noisy simulation.
